title: laborCategory backfill classified technical craft roles containing 'lead'/'chief' (Lead Technician, Chief Engineer) as MANAGER because the MANAGER pass ran before TECHNICAL, skewing labour-cost analytics buckets
rule_violated: A specific craft signal must outrank a generic seniority token (lead/chief) in classification; ordered passes must not let the generic token win.
notes: Wave 4c: the original migration already ran in prod (immutable), so a conservative corrective migration (1802000000000-ReclassifyTechnicalLeads) reclassifies manager rows that carry a craft noun + lead/chief but NO genuine management token and dept != management -> technical. Idempotent, forward-only. The 'senior' vector the review hypothesised does not exist. Analytics-only.

title: HR finance read model couples headcount and salary in one MANAGER+ADMIN-gated payload, so there is no aggregate-only (headcount) tier separable from individual/department salary

title: updateUserRole ran the role-grant authority guard only inside `if (roleId changed)`, so an override-only update skipped it — a delegate holding users:edit_permissions could self-grant any tenant capability (effective next token refresh).

title: No "cannot grant more than you have" invariant and no catalogue whitelist on any tenant-role write path (createRole/updateRole/assignUserRole/updateUserRole/createUser); arbitrary resource:action strings injectable and a delegate could author/assign roles carrying capabilities they did not hold.

title: Tenant-role gating invariant iterated a hand-maintained method-name list, so a newly-added @Query/@Mutation forgotten in the list and left ungated passed CI silently and fell through both opt-in guards to any authenticated tenant user.

title: TenantRoleService carried duplicate, unaudited, unguarded role-lifecycle methods (assignRoleToUser/removeRoleFromUser/setDefaultRole) with no production callers — a latent trap that a future wiring would use to reintroduce the horizontal-escalation and audit-gap holes the live TenantUserManagementService paths close.

title: permissionOverrides.grants/revokes had no length or per-item bound at the validation boundary, so an abusive payload could inflate the request and downstream the JWT resourcePermissions claim + gateway assertion header.

title: A permission REVOKE (role change, override change, role-permission edit) did not take effect until the access-token TTL: nothing invalidated a user live tokens on an authorization change, even though the gateway already enforced the user_blacklist:{userId} Redis key on every request (which had a reader but no writer).

notes: FIXED in the same commit: canonical UserTokenRevocationService in backend-common owns the user_blacklist:{userId} key; auth-service RBAC write paths revoke on committed change (updateRole fans out to holders); the gateway reader shares the userBlacklistKey builder. title: Coverage-mode test run swallowed --coverage at eight producers and cached test tasks without their coverage outputs
rule_violated: A gate must be able to succeed: the coverage-evidence contract required reports from producers whose runner never received the coverage flag
narrative: The ci-full test job runs `npm run test:all -- --coverage`, which becomes `nx run-many --target=test --all --coverage`. Eight Vitest producers defined `test` as an `nx:run-commands` target wrapping `npm run test`. That executor appends forwarded arguments to its command string, producing `npm run test --coverage` — npm reads the flag as one of its own config options and never passes it to Vitest. Those eight ran with coverage off, wrote no report, and the coverage-evidence gate failed on a run in which every test had passed.

The two producers that did emit reports (messaging-module, tenant-admin) declared no `test` target at all and used the target Nx infers from the package.json script, whose executor forwards options correctly.

A second, latent half of the same failure: `test` is a cached target and ci-full restores .nx/cache between runs, but no test target declared the coverage directory among its `outputs`. Nx restores only declared outputs, so a replayed test task left no report behind — the gate would have failed intermittently even after the flag reached the runner.

title: Attendance clock-in test spied on Date.now while the handler reads new Date, so it passed only during the shift window's hours
rule_violated: A test must control the inputs it claims to control; wall-clock time is an input, not an ambient constant
narrative: `ClockInHandler` reads the instant with `new Date()` (line 93). The test set up its clock with `jest.spyOn(Date, 'now')`, and `new Date()` never calls `Date.now()` — so the spy changed nothing and the handler saw the real wall clock.

The handler rejects a clock-in outside the shift window, which for the fixture shift is 07:00-22:00. The assertion therefore passed whenever CI happened to run inside that window and failed on every run outside it. It went red on a 06:31 UTC run and had passed on a 21:11 UTC run of the same code the evening before.

Reproduced deterministically by moving the runner's timezone rather than waiting for the hour: under TZ=Etc/GMT+6 (local 01:00) the failure is identical to CI's, and after faking the system clock the suite is 30/30 under Etc/GMT+6, Etc/GMT-9 and UTC alike.

title: Payroll period numbering and leave half-day arithmetic shift by one calendar unit when the host timezone is behind UTC
rule_violated: Date arithmetic that spans a calendar boundary must be evaluated in a fixed, declared timezone rather than the host's
narrative: Surfaced while reproducing the attendance clock defect by shifting the runner timezone. Under TZ=Etc/GMT+6 the payroll number for a January pay period is generated as PAY-202512 instead of PAY-202601, and the leave half-day path returns 2 days where it should return 1.5.

Both are UTC-versus-local calendar-boundary errors, the same family as the attendance defect but in different code. They are invisible to CI because the runner is UTC, and invisible to the platform only for as long as every deployment stays on UTC — a payroll period attributed to the wrong month is a finance-visible error, not a test artifact.

NOT investigated in this change: whether the production handlers or only the fixtures are wrong. The reproduction is recorded here so the owner starts from evidence rather than rediscovering it; the fix is the owner's, on the deadline set.

notes: Two concurrent activate calls carrying the same valid token (e.g. a cloned SD-card image, or an attacker racing a legitimate boot who holds the installer token) both read tokenUsedAt=null, both pass validation, both enter the transaction, and both save. The 'single-use' guarantee is advisory, not enforced by the database. Result: two distinct MQTT credential sets generated for the same device identity, the second silently overwriting the first, and the single-use invariant is violated.

This mirrors the TOCTOU-safe pattern alrea
title: Device activation is not atomic — single-use provisioning token can be redeemed twice under a race

notes: Many industrial devices publish 32-bit floats/ints in Low-High word order. The RTU adapter exposes a wordOrder config field and schema option but the decoder ignores it, so every LOW_HIGH device yields byte-swapped garbage. The TCP adapter's swap is limited to the first register pair and silently mis-decodes float64 and register arrays. The config schema promises a behaviour the codec does not honor. Because there are no adapter tests (see test-gap finding), this drift is invisible.
rule_violated: category=contract-drift: Replace both hand-rolled parsers with the shared @platform/protocol-codec word/byte-order decode (the same crate the golden spec and base-vfd.calculateCRC16 already use) so endianness/word-order is implemented once and covered by golden fixtures; add golden cases for LOW_HIG
title: Sensor Modbus 32-bit word-order decoding is wrong: modbus-rtu ignores wordOrder entirely; modbus-tcp only swaps the first 2 words

narrative: Reproduced against a live PostgreSQL 16 by calling the production orchestrator directly: runSchemaMigrations({ schema: 'tenant_0000000000000001', migrations: apps/sensor-service/src/database/migrations/[0-9]*, migrationsTableName: 'migrations_sensor' }) — the exact call tenant-schema-provisioner.ts makes at processJob(). Against an EMPTY sensor schema the run created every Baseline table inside `sensor` and none inside the tenant schema; applyTenantRlsToSchema then logged 'No tenant-scoped tables found in schema tenant_0000000000000001 — nothing to do'. Against a sensor schema that already held one Baseline table (the state of any real deployment, where the source schema migrates first) the same call aborted with: relation "sensor_protocols" already exists.

Mechanism: tenant provisioning is migration REPLAY. The orchestrator pins SET search_path TO "<tenant schema>", public before every migration, which routes UNQUALIFIED DDL into the tenant schema. Every Baseline is generated by TypeORM's CLI and is therefore fully schema-qualified ("sensor"."sensors", "farm"."code_sequences", "hr"."payrolls"), so the search_path pin has no effect on it and the DDL re-targets the source schema. The only escape hatch, @SourceOnlyMigration, is applied to exactly one sensor migration and to no Baseline.

Existing tenants are NOT affected: their migrations_<schema> journals were populated by the retired runtime seeder (SchemaManagerService.seedMigrationsHistory), so Baseline is already recorded as applied and replay resumes at the first genuinely-new migration. That is why incremental fan-out works today and why the breakage is invisible until someone provisions a NEW tenant. stray-tenant-journal-heal.ts documents the same coupling from the other side: dropping a tenant journal 'would make the next deploy re-run the full history against that tenant and crash on relation already exists'.

Why no test caught it: bootstrap-from-scratch.spec.ts migrates source schemas only and never provisions a tenant; tenant-schema-provisioner.contract.spec.ts is a text-grep spec with no database; tenant-clone-parity.spec.ts provisions its fixture with CREATE TABLE ... LIKE INCLUDING ALL — the retired runtime mechanism — so it validates a fan-out shape production no longer produces, and its table-set assertion is a tautology because the spec itself is the fan-out. tests/invariants/tenant-aware-migration-ddl-guard.spec.ts would catch the qualified DDL but filters Baseline out of its own file list with no stated reason.

Fix direction (needs its own PR + architectural-arbiter review): either make every tenant-aware Baseline replay-safe (unqualified DDL for per-tenant tables, @SourceOnlyMigration for the cross-tenant ones), or have the provisioner seed a new tenant's journal from the source ledger up to the Baseline head before replaying — the behaviour the retired seeder used to provide. Whichever is chosen, the gate is a live-database test that provisions a tenant through the real provisioner and asserts a non-empty, correctly-shaped tenant schema; the current countTenantTables > 0 check inside the provisioner already fails loudly, so this is broken-and-noisy rather than silently-wrong.
notes: Found while verifying that migration 1815000000000-CreateTenantSensorMetricsHypertable actually reaches tenant schemas. It does — for EXISTING tenants, whose journals already record Baseline, so the replay resumes and runs the new unqualified migration in each tenant schema as designed. New-tenant provisioning is a separate, pre-existing platform break that predates this branch and affects all seven tenant-aware services equally, so it is tracked rather than folded into the sensor PR: the fix touches eight Baselines or the provisioner's journal-seeding contract, needs architectural-arbiter sign-off on which of the two, and cannot be validated without a live provisioning run. narrative: `format check-changed` resolves its base from FORMAT_BASE_SHA and falls back to `HEAD^` when that variable is unset. CI sets it to the pull request's base, so CI checks every file the branch touches; a developer running the same command locally checks only the last commit. On this branch that was 67 files locally versus 195 in CI.

The consequence is not theoretical: 35 files added by this branch were never Prettier-formatted, the local gate reported success on every run, and the drift only surfaced when CI - Full first ran on the branch. New files are the worst case, because they have no base blob and are counted as regressions outright.

The 35 files are formatted in this change. The gate itself is NOT fixed here: making the local default match CI means resolving the merge-base against the default branch, which changes behaviour for every developer and belongs to the tooling owner. Recorded with owner infra-expert and deadline 2026-09-15 rather than patched in a sensor PR.
rule_violated: A gate a developer can run locally must evaluate the same thing CI evaluates, or it provides false assurance
title: Format gate checks a different, far narrower base locally than in CI, so a branch can look clean and still fail the required check

narrative: The test mints a JWT with `exp: Math.floor(Date.now()/1000) + 1` and asserts the guard accepts it. Because `now` is floored to whole seconds, the token's real remaining life is anywhere from ~1000ms down to ~0ms, and the guard is genuinely correct to reject it once that elapses. The assertion therefore measures runner speed, not the expiry boundary.

It failed in CI - Full at 08:24 UTC with `UnauthorizedException: Invalid or expired token`; the same suite took 40.6s under coverage instrumentation. It passed on an earlier run of identical gateway-api code, so it is load-dependent rather than broken code.

Proved by controlled comparison rather than by observing it pass once: with a 1.5s delay injected between minting the token and calling the guard, the unpinned test reproduces CI's exact error, and the pinned-clock version passes. Only `Date` is faked so the guard's real asynchronous work still settles.
rule_violated: A test must not depend on how much real time elapses between its setup and its assertion
title: AuthGuard token-expiry test asserted the runner's speed rather than the guard's boundary, and failed once the suite got slower

narrative: CI - Full's build job failed on bc96b2d1a with `Running target build for 39 projects failed` and two names: router-coprocessor:build and protocol-codec-rs:build. Across the whole job log neither name appears anywhere else — no Compiling line, no rustc diagnostic, no exit status. Nx printed the summary and discarded the tasks' output.

The evidence says the code was never the problem. The commit contains zero Rust or Cargo files (33 .ts, 2 .md, 1 .tsx, 1 .jsonl, 1 .json); both crates build clean locally; the same build job passed on the parent commit minutes earlier; and on this exact SHA all eleven dedicated Rust jobs passed, including cargo test --workspace, cargo clippy -D warnings, cargo check, cross-build (musl) for two targets, and the compile + test-compile gate.

What the mechanism actually was remains unknown, and that is the finding. There is no OOM evidence in the log — the `signal` and `137` matches are crate names and version strings, not a kill signal or exit code. A task that dies without emitting a line is not a compiler rejection, but the job as configured cannot tell anyone which of the possibilities it was, so the next occurrence will cost the same investigation. Making the build job stream or retain per-task output is the fix; it belongs to the workflow's owner rather than to a sensor PR.
rule_violated: A failing CI job must surface why it failed; a task name with no captured output is not a diagnosis
title: A failing Nx task in CI Full's build job reports its name and nothing else, so every failure costs a full investigation

title: The pre-commit hook mirrors only one of CI's two format gates: `format check-changed` has no local counterpart, so eight commits shipped Prettier drift before CI objected
rule_violated: A gate that blocks merge in CI must have a local counterpart that fires earlier, or the local mirror is a false assurance. Mirroring one of a pair and claiming the pair is covered is worse than mirroring neither, because the developer stops looking.
notes: FOUND BY CI, not by review -- which is itself the point. PR #1024's first real CI run (30495813228, head 300526134) went red on `lint-and-typecheck` step 10, `quality.mjs format check-changed`, with ten Prettier-drifted files, every one of them authored in this session: docs/plans/2026-06-18-enterprise-grade-debt-closure/finding-truth-table.md, docs/plans/2026-07-26-aria-software-team-program/PLAN.md, docs/reviews/2026-07-26-aria-codex-audit-verification.md, tests/invariants/workflow-npm-script-references.spec.ts, and six tools/gates files (aria-authority-hash.ts, commit-msg-validator.ts, finding-registry.ts, finding-registry-store.ts, finding-registry-store.spec.ts, repin-debt-plan.ts). ROOT CAUSE: CI runs TWO format gates -- `format-scope check` (manifest freshness) and `format check-changed` (actual drift) -- and .husky/pre-commit runs only the first. The hook's own comment states the intent exactly: 'Push sonrasi CI kirmizisi yerine commit aninda yakala (tier-3 make-it-detectable)'. So the intent was written down and half-implemented; the gate that catches drift has no local counterpart at all. MEASURED CONSEQUENCE: eight commits on this branch shipped drift with a green pre-commit hook every time. This is the SAME DEFECT CLASS the branch exists to close (ORPHAN-HIGH-455: a control written, tested, exported, and not wired where it matters) in mirror image -- here the CI side is wired and the local mirror is the half that is missing. SECOND-ORDER DEFECT: quality.mjs offers modes `check | check-changed | write` and no `write-changed`, so the only one-command fix a developer can reach for is repo-wide `format write`, which rewrites every managed file including the ~28 that check-changed deliberately quarantines as pre-existing base debt -- burying a 10-file fix in 38 files of churn. The missing write mode is why the drift was tedious to fix correctly and therefore likely to be fixed incorrectly. FIX (tier 2 + tier 3): extract the regression-set computation out of runPrettierChanged into a shared computeFormatRegressions(base); add a `write-changed` mode over exactly that set; add a staged-mode drift check to .husky/pre-commit (staged, not the HEAD^ fallback, because at pre-commit time the content under test is uncommitted so HEAD^ is the wrong base); and pin the mirror with an invariant asserting every quality.mjs gate in ci-full.yml's lint-and-typecheck job has a pre-commit counterpart or a stated exemption. Without the last part this is a one-time repair of a recurring class. NOTE ON BLAST RADIUS, verified not assumed: reformatting these ten files does not move the ARIA authority hash -- AUTHORITY_ROOTS is ['docs/aria','aria-kernel','tools/aria-poc'] (aria-authority-hash.ts:67) and none of the ten fall under it; and repin-debt-plan.ts anchors are fail-closed via substituteOrThrow (:112), so a moved anchor fails loudly rather than corrupting a mirror. title: lint-and-typecheck exceeds its 15-minute budget after the merge, so the job is cancelled before its last two gates run — the format check has not executed in CI-Full on any recent head
rule_violated: A gate job's time budget must exceed its measured workload with headroom. When it does not, the job is cancelled at whatever step it reached and every later step reports `skipped` — the gates at the tail of the job stop running while the job still looks like a configured gate.
notes: MEASURED, not inferred. ci-full.yml:39 sets `timeout-minutes: 15` on lint-and-typecheck. On head 5967d7285 (run 30520580511) the job started 06:45:42 and was cancelled 07:00:55 — 15m13s — inside step 9 `Run type-check-spec gate`, with step 10 `Check formatting of changed files` reported `skipped`. No push followed 5967d7285, so this was the job timeout and not the concurrency cancel-in-progress that killed the previous run. Step timings: linter 8m57s (06:47:02-06:55:59), type check 3m8s (06:55:59-06:59:07), plus ~1.3m setup/install/rust. type-check-spec needs ~1.9m (measured 06:31:11-06:33:08 on run 30495813228) and the format check ~16s, so the job needs ~17.5m against a 15m budget. WHY IT CHANGED: on head 300526134 the same job completed in 12m25s with the linter taking 6m36s. The merge of main added the @aquaculture/testing workspace, so `nx run-many --target=lint` covers more projects and the linter grew to 8m57s, tipping the job over its limit. CONSEQUENCE, and it is the part that matters: a cancelled job runs none of its remaining steps, so BOTH tail gates silently stop executing. `Check formatting of changed files` shows `skipped` on runs 30520045513 and 30520580511 — the gate whose absence from the pre-commit hook is ORPHAN-HIGH-500 is now also not running in CI, one layer up. The safety property still holds (build-status treats cancelled as not-success and fails closed, so nothing merges), but the diagnosis is actively misleading: build-status prints `Lint/Typecheck failed`, which sends the reader to look for a lint error that does not exist. FIX: raise the budget to fit the measured workload with headroom, consistent with the file's own conventions (test 30, build 30, deploy-ssot-gates 20). NOT FIXED HERE, and deliberately separated: the job does four heavy serial passes (lint all, tsc all, a second full tsc pass in type-check-spec, format) and splitting them into parallel jobs would be the better design, but the job names are wired into the `build-status` aggregate and into the required-status-check manifest, so renaming or splitting them touches branch protection and belongs in its own change with the ruleset updated in lockstep. title: The pre-PR-open perimeter authorised dry runs and fed their stage-artifact refusals to the failure breaker, so putting the phase on the live lane would have made the nightly halt itself on its own observations
rule_violated: An observation must not be able to trip a safety breaker. A gate evaluated where the mutation cannot happen is reporting on the stage, not judging the action, and counting its refusals as rejected implementations turns telemetry into a halt condition.
notes: PREVENTATIVE, and the sequencing is the point: this had to land BEFORE RC-1, not after. open_pr_for_action runs the 10-check GATE_PRE_PR_OPEN perimeter before its dry_run branch, deliberately, so a preview cannot skip the gate. But a dry run opens nothing: no changed_files, no base_sha, no diff. Checks needing those refused on data that CANNOT exist at that stage, and cycle.py's _run_pr_lifecycle_phase fed every refusal whose message started with PERIMETER_REFUSED_PREFIX to record_failure(kind='validator_rejection'). Three approved_for_apply proposals in one cycle would trip a breaker that ORPHAN-CRITICAL-420 S2 extended to gate `standard` -- the profile the nightly runs. The lane would halt itself on its own telemetry. It has never fired only because _run_extended_phases is unreachable (ORPHAN-CRITICAL-498), and RC-1 exists to put that phase on the live lane. FIX, tier 1 rather than a flag: the mode is the RESULT TYPE. observe_perimeter() returns a PerimeterObservation with no `passed`, no `failures` and no `raise_if_blocked`, so there is no attribute a breaker producer can read as a refusal; run_hard_fail_checks() keeps its HardFailReport and its fail-closed semantics for real opens. Both run the SAME registry through one implementation, so an observation and an authorisation can never disagree about what a check does. PerimeterVerdict adds a third state, not_evaluable_at_this_stage, distinct from passed=False -- the collapse of those two is what made a dry run look like a rejected implementation. TWO CORRECT ARGUMENTS WERE IN TENSION and neither was discarded: the pre-RC-2 design ran the authorising gate before the dry_run branch so a preview could not report ok while the perimeter would block (a false green), while RC-2 requires that a preview not be counted as a refusal. `evaluable` separates them: a preview is STILL refused when a check that could run refused (self-modification, secret in diff, unsigned commit) and is NOT refused when the only refusals name inputs the stage cannot supply. THE BREAKER IS NOT LEFT WITHOUT A PRODUCER: planner_dispatch_hook records subprocess_timeout from a single except arm, discriminated structurally rather than by message prefix, so ORPHAN-CRITICAL-485 stays closed -- and an invariant pins that, precisely so nobody restores the removed edge believing the breaker went decorative again. ENFORCEMENT: tests/invariants/v3/test_perimeter_observe_has_no_breaker_edge.py, six AST assertions (not grep -- grep is what reported ORPHAN-CRITICAL-428 as wired, and this fix's own comments name record_failure, so a substring version would fail on its documentation). Proven to bite: restoring the edge fails 2 of 6 with the diagnostic naming the phase. Also removed the imports orphaned by the deletion -- an import left behind after its call is what made ORPHAN-HIGH-499's mutation invisible to a hasattr test. The four new public symbols were registered in the v9 __all__ pin rather than the pin being relaxed: that invariant exists to make an API addition a review event. title: A static reachability invariant cannot catch a kwarg-gated dead pipeline, so the RC-1 tier-3 control does not subsume the tier-1 collapse it was planned alongside
rule_violated: A detection control must be honest about the class of defect it cannot see. Shipping a reachability invariant while the plan describes it as 'the generalised answer to the defect class' would leave readers believing the class is closed when its most expensive instance is invisible to the tool.
notes: FOUND BY BUILDING THE TOOL THE PLAN ASKED FOR. RC-1 specifies a static call-graph reachability invariant and calls it 'the generalised answer to the defect class... the piece that would have caught 494, 495, 497 and the two lens CRITICALs without a review cycle'. It would not have caught ORPHAN-CRITICAL-498, and the reason is structural rather than an implementation gap: a CONDITIONAL call is still an edge. `run_enterprise_cycle` really does call `_run_extended_phases` in the source; the call is guarded by `if run_phases is not None` and no production caller passes the kwarg. Any static walk therefore reports the entire extended pipeline as reachable while it never executes. This is not fixable by improving the resolver -- deciding whether that branch is entered is the halting problem in miniature. CONSEQUENCE FOR SEQUENCING: the tier-3 invariant and the tier-1 collapse cover DIFFERENT failures and neither substitutes for the other. The invariant catches a control with no caller at all (ORPHAN-CRITICAL-420's breaker, whose only occurrence was its own def). The registry catches a control whose caller is never entered (498). Shipping only the invariant and treating RC-1 as closed would leave the more expensive half open under a green test -- the exact shape of the defect class. TWO FALSE POSITIVES ON THE WAY, both from the resolver and both fixed rather than exempted, because a reachability tool that over-reports teaches its readers to ignore it: (1) `record_failure` reported dead, actually reached through callback indirection -- autonomous_planner_dispatcher assigns `invoke_planner = dispatch_one_pending_planner_request` and calls the local, so following imports alone loses the edge; fixed by following single Name = Name aliases. (2) `assert_autonomy_unlocked` reported dead, actually reached through a Protocol-typed strategy OBJECT -- cli -> select_auto_merge_runner -> RealAutoMergeRunner(...) -> runner(...) -> __call__ -> merge_pr_if_ready; fixed by giving a resolved constructor call an edge to that class's __call__, scoped to __call__ alone rather than to every method. Both corrections are documented at the code that makes them. A false accusation is as damaging as a missed defect: acting on either would have meant re-wiring a control that was already wired. CURRENT STATE: all five declared safety controls are reachable from a production entry point, so the invariant's value today is preventing regression, not repairing a present defect. REMAINING WORK, tier 1, design settled and unstarted: a CyclePhase record (name, runner, precondition drawn from an enumerated set), a CYCLE_PHASES ordered tuple as SSoT with pr_lifecycle present under precondition profile_in(PROFILES_WITH_ACTION_AUTHORITY), a uniform PhaseContext so one loop can invoke runners whose signatures currently differ, run_enterprise_cycle iterating that tuple, and run_phases / pre_tool_phases DELETED rather than kept as a compatibility seam -- a second entrance to the same phases is how this happened. Five test files pass those kwargs and migrate with it. Not started in this commit because a half-collapsed pipeline is worse than an uncollapsed one, and the invariant above is what will define 'done' for it: once the kwargs are gone, phase membership is a data question the registry answers. title: DEFAULT_CYCLE_PHASES declares 5 phases while run_enterprise_cycle runs 15, and one declared name does not match what the body emits, so the phase constants validate a kwarg nobody passes against a list that misdescribes the cycle
rule_violated: A constant that names the steps of a pipeline is either the pipeline's SSoT or it is misinformation. Keeping it as input validation for an argument no production caller passes gives it the appearance of authority with none of the responsibility, and any registry built on it inherits the error.
notes: FOUND WHILE SCOPING RC-1's TIER-1 COLLAPSE, and it changes that work's shape rather than merely adding to it. ACTUALLY RUN by run_enterprise_cycle's body, enumerated from its own emit_progress calls and post_tool_failure phase labels: belief_decay, consensus_escalation, discovery, human_required_adjudication, judge_calibration, learning_post_evidence_closure, lease_lifecycle_escalation, memory, metrics, observability_dashboard, pressure, proactive_priority, reflection, service_examination, tools -- fifteen, not five. NAME MISMATCH ON TOP: the constant says 'discover' while the body emits 'discovery', so even the one-word overlap is not exact. WHAT THE CONSTANTS ARE FOR: SUPPORTED_CYCLE_PHASES exists only to validate the run_phases / pre_tool_phases kwargs at function entry (cycle.py ~268-281). Those kwargs have no production caller (ORPHAN-CRITICAL-498), so the pair validates input nobody passes, against a phase list that does not describe the cycle. It has the appearance of a phase SSoT and none of the duties of one. CONSEQUENCE FOR RC-1: the plan specifies 'a CYCLE_PHASES ordered tuple as the SSoT' and implicitly treats the existing constant as the set to formalise. Building the registry from those five names would encode the wrong pipeline and leave ten phases outside the SSoT that is supposed to be authoritative -- a duplicate representation, which is the failure the collapse exists to remove. The registry has to be derived from the body's real phases, which makes the collapse materially larger than 'move four extended phases behind preconditions': it is a restructuring of ~300 lines of inline sequential phase code, each block with its own try/except and post_tool_failure assignment. NOT STARTED, deliberately, and this finding is why: a registry built on a constant I have just proven wrong would be worse than no registry. The correct order is (1) settle what the phase set actually is, (2) build CyclePhase / CYCLE_PHASES from that set with enumerated preconditions and an explicit pre_tool/post_tool stage field replacing the two kwargs, (3) delete run_phases, pre_tool_phases, DEFAULT_CYCLE_PHASES and SUPPORTED_CYCLE_PHASES together -- the kwargs and the constants that validate them are one unit and removing either alone leaves a dangling half. A SEPARATE RISK the collapse must handle rather than discover: the four extended phases have NEVER executed in production. Putting them on the live lane runs pr_lifecycle -> open_pr_for_action on every cycle carrying approved_for_apply proposals. ORPHAN-CRITICAL-503 removed the breaker edge so this can no longer self-halt the nightly, but it is still a first-time behaviour change on a scheduled lane and needs its precondition (profile_in(PROFILES_WITH_ACTION_AUTHORITY)) to be right before it is switched on, not after. title: One undecodable row in the failure ledger trips the breaker permanently: dropped_rows never ages out of the sliding window and the only recovery lever also destroyed the agent queue
rule_violated: A fail-closed safety state must be exitable without discarding evidence. A state that can only be left by deleting the evidence is an outage wearing a safety property's clothes, and it teaches operators to reach for the destructive lever.
notes: MECHANISM, and the ordering that causes it is itself correct. evaluate_breaker decides evidence_incomplete BEFORE the threshold comparison, which is what ORPHAN-CRITICAL-418 fixed: unreadable evidence must not read as permissive. But BreakerEvidence.dropped_rows = max(0, rows_present - len(rows)) counts lines that failed to DECODE, while _count_failures_in_window only ages the lines that DID decode. A corrupt line is therefore outside time: it can never leave the window. One truncated row in aria-tools/breakers/autonomous-failures.jsonl trips the breaker for every subsequent nightly `standard` cycle, permanently. Asserted rather than argued in the new test: re-stamping the surviving row a year into the past leaves the verdict at evidence_incomplete. COMPOUNDING FACTOR: the ledger travels between runs inside the aria-tools-state artifact, and `aria-kernel breaker reset` operates on a local --tools-dir. So the operator's only effective lever was deleting the artifact -- which also destroys the agent-invocation queue ORPHAN-CRITICAL-469 exists to carry. The recovery path for one breaker was the destruction of an unrelated subsystem. FIX, first half, landed: quarantine_breaker_evidence() moves ONLY undecodable rows to a sidecar (verbatim, with an operator-attributed header), keeps every decodable row BYTE-FOR-BYTE, and does NOT touch the state file. The breaker re-derives from the survivors. So the state becomes EVALUABLE, not clear -- and the test that matters asserts exactly that: three real in-window failures plus one corrupt line quarantines to a breaker that is STILL tripped, now with reason threshold_exceeded, which is what the operator needed to see all along. A reset would have cleared both, which is why this is a different verb rather than a flag on reset: an operator reaching for 'make the breaker evaluable' must not land on 'discard the evidence'. It refuses on a count mismatch between its own per-line partition and the breaker's own read_strict_jsonl reader, because rewriting the ledger against a different definition of decodable than the evaluator uses would be two sites disagreeing about one file. It refuses outright when the ledger is unreadable -- that is a file-access fault, not row damage, and rewriting a file we could not read would be writing over evidence never seen. It gets a CLI (`aria-kernel breaker quarantine --acknowledge --reason ... --operator-approval-ref ...`) because ORPHAN-HIGH-465 was precisely an operator-recovery function shipped with no command surface; exit 1 when the breaker is still tripped afterwards, so a still-blocked lane cannot read as a finished recovery. NOT DONE, second half: recovery still runs where the state ISN'T. The CLI operates on a local --tools-dir while the live ledger lives in the artifact, so an operator cannot yet quarantine the deployed ledger. The design is a workflow_dispatch input on aria-agent-executor performing restore -> mutate -> republish THROUGH THE EXISTING S1 BRIDGE (ORPHAN-CRITICAL-469) -- explicitly not a second restore path, because a duplicate transaction around a hash-chained ledger is how the ledger diverges. Not implemented here because it needs a live artifact round-trip to verify and this container cannot reach the GitHub API; shipping it unverified would be the untested-callsite defect this whole branch exists to close. [canonicalize-owner 2026-10-18: owner_user okan -> Okan-wqm — ARIA-MEDIUM-535 owner identity is the CODEOWNERS handle]

title: The spec type-check ratchet enumerated three hardcoded roots and so never covered tests/invariants: 24 pre-existing type errors in the files that enforce every other platform rule were invisible to every gate
rule_violated: A gate's coverage set must be derived from the property that makes something coverable, not from a hand-maintained list of places to look. An enumerated root list is a log of the times someone noticed, so the first directory nobody noticed is silently ungated — and the gate still reports OK.
notes: FOUND BY CHASING A SYMPTOM I HAD MIS-DIAGNOSED. Earlier in this session I flagged that 'two type gates disagree about one tree' after CI - Full's type-check step passed on commit 4aa3309e1 while Quality Gates' type-check job failed with three noUncheckedIndexedAccess errors in tests/invariants/git-hook-binding.spec.ts. On investigation the scopes are DELIBERATE and layered, not contradictory: tools/scripts/type-check-all.mjs covers app/lib COMPILE tsconfigs and documents that it excludes .spec.json ('tests are a separate concern'); gates:type-check-spec owns spec tsconfigs as a baseline-aware ratchet; ci-affected's scripts/ci/type-check-changed-files.mjs covers CHANGED files anywhere. So my original framing was wrong and is withdrawn. THE REAL DEFECT, one layer down: type-check-spec.ts discoverProjects() enumerated roots = ['apps','libs','platform/libs'], and its own comment recorded that platform/libs had been appended the first time a platform lib grew a spec config -- which is the tell. The list is a log of the times someone noticed. MEASURED: the repo holds 30 tsconfig.spec.json files; those three roots reach 29. The one missed is tests/invariants -- the directory holding the invariants that enforce every other rule in the platform, so the ratchet that guards spec type errors was blind to the specs that guard everything else. CONSEQUENCE: a type error there was caught only by ci-affected's changed-files guard, which sees a file when it CHANGES and never guards the rest, so a PRE-EXISTING error was invisible to every gate. That is exactly why my own error surfaced in one lane and not the other. FIX: discoverProjects() now DERIVES the project set from the presence of a tsconfig.spec.json via a depth-bounded walk, stopping descent at a project so a nested fixture config cannot register as its own entry. A new top-level tree is covered the moment it acquires a spec config, with no second place to remember to edit. Proven to bite on the newly covered project: injecting one error reports 'tests/invariants 25 (baseline 24, +1) regressed' and fails the gate. WHAT WAS NOT DONE, and why. Widening the gate revealed 24 pre-existing errors across SIX invariant files I did not write (aria-workflow-sha-pin, rls-predicate-canonical, pii-events-mandatory-crypto-shred, migration-registration-completeness, event-contract-emit-has-interface, dead-contract-fe-operations), all of the same class: undefined-not-assignable under noUncheckedIndexedAccess. They are recorded as the project's baseline (24), which is the ratchet's designed onboarding path and identical to how 11 of 20 projects were onboarded when the gate was introduced. That makes 24 invisible errors into 24 tracked-and-capped errors -- a strict improvement and tier 3, NOT tier 1. The errors themselves are not fixed: doing it correctly means reading six unfamiliar invariant files, and the shortcuts available (non-null assertions, casts) are banned by CLAUDE.md and would be worse than the debt. Owner and deadline recorded here for that cleanup; the ratchet guarantees the number cannot grow while it waits. [canonicalize-owner 2026-10-18: owner_user okan -> Okan-wqm — ARIA-MEDIUM-535 owner identity is the CODEOWNERS handle]

title: No local git hook type-checked anything: pre-commit ran staged-only gates and pre-push ran only Rust clippy, so a TypeScript error could only be discovered by CI
rule_violated: A gate that blocks merge in CI needs a local counterpart that fires earlier, and the parity mechanism that enforces this must cover every kind of gate — not one family. A parity invariant that understands only one gate type teaches its readers that parity is enforced everywhere.
notes: MEASURED CONSEQUENCE, from this session. A noUncheckedIndexedAccess error in tests/invariants/git-hook-binding.spec.ts reached CI on PR #1024 head 4aa3309e1 and failed the type-check job, taking merge-gate and sens-enterprise-summary down with it as derivatives. I had verified the file with jest, which transpiles without full type-checking, so the suite was green while tsc --noEmit was not. No local hook could have caught it: .husky/pre-commit runs staged-only banned-phrase/construct/migration/tier-claim gates plus the format gate, and .husky/pre-push ran ONE thing -- tools/gates/clippy-affected.ts. TypeScript had no local gate at all. Same missing-local-mirror shape as ORPHAN-HIGH-500, one gate over. FIX, and the choice of WHICH gate to mirror is the architectural part. Platform-wide `npm run type-check` takes ~2.5 minutes; adding that to every push makes people look for ways around the hook, and a hook people bypass is worse than no hook. So the mirror is the gate that actually catches this class in CI: ci-affected's scripts/ci/type-check-changed-files.mjs. Its cost is proportional to the change and its scope is exactly the risky set. Wired into pre-push, which is the correct stage because the script compares a COMMITTED range (origin/main..HEAD) -- pre-commit content is not committed yet, so the same script there would compare the wrong pair. When origin/main cannot be resolved it skips LOUDLY, printing why: a base that cannot be computed means 'changed' is undefined, and blocking an offline branch push would be wrong -- but skipping silently is the blind-gate defect this session already fixed once, so the reason is printed and CI remains the authority. SECOND HALF OF THE FIX, and the reason this finding is not just 'add a hook line': the parity invariant added for ORPHAN-HIGH-500 understood only `quality.mjs <domain> <action>` gates. It enforced parity for exactly one family and silently ignored every other kind of CI gate -- the same shape as ORPHAN-HIGH-507's hardcoded root list, one layer up. It now also asserts a declared set of SCRIPT gates, matched on script PATH rather than command line so a hook passing different arguments than CI (pre-push uses --base origin/main; CI uses the PR base ref) still counts as the mirror. The set is declared rather than 'every script any workflow runs', because most CI steps -- builds, uploads, container setup -- have no business in a git hook and asserting they do would make the invariant noise; what belongs is a gate that REFUSES a change on a property a developer could have checked locally. Proven to bite: deleting the pre-push line fails the new assertion naming the script and the reason it exists. [canonicalize-owner 2026-10-18: owner_user okan -> Okan-wqm — ARIA-MEDIUM-535 owner identity is the CODEOWNERS handle]

title: The workflow-injection invariant matched only the legacy ${{ github.event.inputs.X }} spelling, so a run: block interpolating the modern ${{ inputs.X }} shorthand passed a green gate
rule_violated: A gate that recognises one spelling of the construct it forbids enforces half its rule while reporting full compliance. Where a language offers two syntaxes for the same value, the gate must match the VALUE, not the syntax someone happened to write when the gate was authored.
notes: FOUND BY DISTRUSTING MY OWN GREEN RESULT. While adding the RC-9 capability probe I wrote `echo "${{ inputs.runner_label }}"` inside a run: block -- textbook shell injection of operator-supplied text. The repo HAS an invariant for exactly this (Plan 024 v3 B-3, aria-workflow-input-injection.spec.ts) and it PASSED on my file. Rather than accept the pass I checked why, expecting the same hardcoded-list defect as ORPHAN-HIGH-507. It was not that -- the spec scans every workflow via readdirSync, which is correct. The defect was the pattern: INPUTS_INTERPOLATION_RE matched only /\$\{\{\s*github\.event\.inputs\.[A-Za-z0-9_]+\s*\}\}/, the LEGACY spelling. GitHub also offers `${{ inputs.X }}` as the modern workflow_dispatch shorthand; both splice the same attacker-controlled value into the same shell, and the gate recognised one of them. So the invariant reported compliance on a file that violated the rule it exists to enforce. FIXED IN THE SAME CHANGE as the workflow that exposed it: the pattern now matches both spellings, the offending workflow passes its input through an `env:` block and references "$VAR" (the canonical fix the spec's own docstring prescribes), and the test TITLE was corrected too -- it named only `${{ github.event.inputs.* }}`, which is the same misinformation one layer up: a reader scanning test names would conclude the modern spelling was out of scope by design. Proven to bite both ways: with the fix in place the suite is green, and restoring `${{ inputs.runner_label }}` inside the run: block fails the invariant with the file, line and matched snippet. RESIDUAL, stated because it bounds the fix: the invariant's scope is deliberately limited to aria-* workflows (its docstring says non-ARIA workflows are tracked separately as ORPHAN-HIGH findings for the platform-CI plan). This change widens WHICH SPELLINGS are caught, not WHICH FILES are scanned, so a non-ARIA workflow interpolating either spelling is still outside this gate -- unchanged by this fix and not silently implied to be covered. [canonicalize-owner 2026-10-18: owner_user okan -> Okan-wqm — ARIA-MEDIUM-535 owner identity is the CODEOWNERS handle]

title: The ARIA kernel suite is the gate that catches ARIA regressions and it had no local counterpart of any kind, so both git hooks reported green on a commit with four red tests and that commit was pushed
rule_violated: CLAUDE.md's 'never commit with red tests' is a rule about outcomes, and an outcome rule with no mechanism behind it is enforced by whoever happens to remember. A CI gate whose failures are only visible after a push is a gate the author learns about from the wrong side of history they cannot rewrite.
notes: FOUND BY MY OWN VIOLATION, one increment after the fact. Before committing RC-9 I ran `npm run invariants:fast` (jest) and `findings:verify`, saw green, committed and PUSHED. The first thing I ran in the NEXT increment was `npm run aria:test:unit`, and four tests were red on the commit already at origin: test_every_actions_use_is_sha_pinned (my composite action's `uses: ./...` has no SHA to pin), test_i_sbx_01_and_02_dispatching_workflows_declare_containment (the install+verify pair moved into the composite action, so neither workflow's own text declares containment any more), and both workflow-preflight contract tests (the new probe workflow was not in the contract registry). Every one of those is a CORRECT finding by a gate doing its job; the defect is that nothing local ran it. WHY THE EXISTING PARITY INVARIANT DID NOT COVER IT, stated because the near-miss matters: tests/invariants/git-hook-binding.spec.ts asserts parity for the ci-full.yml lint-and-typecheck job, and `aria:test:unit` runs in aria-operational-proof.yml. Its scope was stated honestly, so this is a gap rather than a false claim -- but its SCRIPT_GATES map keyed each gate by one path and demanded that same string appear in both a workflow and a hook, which structurally limited it to gates whose CI and local spellings are identical. The gate that mattered most is not one of those: a hook cannot mirror `npm run aria:test:unit` verbatim, because 215 unconditional seconds on every push is how a gate gets bypassed. FIX. scripts/ci/aria-suite-changed.mjs runs the suite only when the commits THIS push adds touch a surface the suite asserts on -- aria-kernel/, tools/aria-poc/, .github/workflows/ and .github/actions/. The last two are in the trigger set because RC-9 broke the suite without touching a line of Python. Scoping decides WHETHER to run, never WHICH tests: the kernel suite is all-or-nothing and a per-file selection would report green on what it skipped. SCRIPT_GATES now carries separate `ci` and `local` tokens so a gate whose mirror is deliberately a different command is still checked. Proven both ways: green with the hook line present, and with it deleted the invariant names the missing mirror. title: The architecture spine gate has never run in production either: both its phases require a plan_id and no production caller supplies one, so the collapse turns an invisible absence into a recorded skip rather than into an execution

title: Every invariant dormancy waiver expired 2026-06-30 and none was enforced: the reachability spec validated the FORMAT of expires_on and never compared it to the clock
rule_violated: An expiry field exists to force a review. If nothing compares it to the date, it is documentation shaped like a control -- and checking the syntax of a date instead of the date is the same error as checking the syntax of a rule instead of the rule.
notes: FOUND BY ADDING ONE SPEC. tests/invariants/aria-single-restore-path.spec.ts was written, passed when run directly, and ran under NO command: all three jest projects used explicit testMatch file lists, and a new file matches none of them. `jest --listTests` returned 179 against 204 spec files on disk. (1) The date is load-bearing: a waiver past its expiry fails. (2) Shard membership is a glob, so a spec is IN the suite because it exists, and the dormancy manifest becomes the ONE exclusion list -- the jest config reads it, so a config list and a manifest can no longer disagree. (3) Every waiver must name a tracked finding: owner + reason + expiry says who, why and until when, but without an ID nothing gets worked, which is how 25 waivers reached one shared date and passed it together. MEASURED OUTCOME, and it is why this was worth doing rather than re-dating. Making the date load-bearing expired all 25 at once. THREE OTHER SPECS PINNED THE ENUMERATION AS CONFIG TEXT and failed on the glob -- critical-infra-ssot, backup-production-secrets, and this file itself. All three now assert the property, because the obvious way to make that failure go away is to put the filename back in a list, which is the wrong direction. title: The 2026-05-18 migration squash dropped DDL that four SSoT layers still declare, and the invariants guarding it read the .archive/ directory, so one reported green off a migration the runtime never applies
rule_violated: Evidence for an invariant must come from what the runtime executes. A gate reporting compliance off a retired file is worse than no gate: it is a standing claim that something is protected when it is not.
notes: FOUND BY CHECKING RC-6's PRECONDITION, then following the thread. Four services squashed their migrations into a Baseline on 2026-05-18 and moved 55 originals to src/.../migrations/.archive/. The constraint exists ONLY in the archive. A freshly migrated database has no such FK. Its sibling test in the SAME FILE pinned one filename and failed with an ENOENT naming a file, which is why the breakage read as a stale test rather than as a missing constraint. SECOND DROP, SAME CAUSE. shared.access_logs is created by no live migration, while AccessLogMiddleware writes a row per request (wired into gateway-api and admin-api-service), AccessLogEntity maps it, protected-tables.ts lists it, and the RLS infrastructure-ledger SSoT declares it. Its guard, access-log-stream-shape.spec.ts, read the migration by hardcoded filename and so failed to LOAD rather than reporting the table gone -- and it was dormant, so nobody saw even that. FIX, TWO PARTS. (1) MECHANISM: tests/invariants/lib/migration-corpus.ts is the one answer to 'which migrations does service X apply?', deriving each service's migrations directory from its own data-source.ts (services disagree: src/migrations for four, src/database/migrations for ten) and excluding anything not directly in it. The helper refuses rather than guessing when a service's declaration cannot be parsed. (2) THE DDL: forward-only restorations -- RestoreAuthUsersTenantFk1807300000000 (with the orphan pre-flight the original carried) and RestoreSharedAccessLogs1801600000000. Both idempotent, so an environment that still has them is unaffected. PROOF THE FIX IS REAL: with the specs on the corpus and the restorations absent, both fail; with the restorations tracked, both pass. The FK assertion in particular went from passing-on-dead-evidence to failing, which is the correct intermediate state and the thing that proves the old green was false. title: The baseline squash hand-authored a fifth audit-immutability variant that refuses ALL deletes, breaking audit retention on three tables and dropping shared.audit_logs protection entirely
rule_violated: A stricter rule is not a safer rule. An append-only guarantee that also forbids lawful expiry converts a compliance control into an unbounded-growth defect, and it does so while looking like hardening.
notes: The pre-squash contract was TWO triggers per audit table: <schema>.<table>_prevent_update (BEFORE UPDATE, always raises) and <schema>.<table>_prevent_legal_hold_delete (BEFORE DELETE, raises ONLY when OLD."legalHold" is true, else RETURN OLD). The second is what lets audit retention expire rows while legal hold blocks it -- the retention module's own docstring names this trigger as its database-level backstop behind the application-layer legalHold = false filter. The Baseline carries a hand-authored single function per table, <schema>.<table>_prevent_update_or_delete, raising on BEFORE UPDATE OR DELETE unconditionally. That is not a stricter version of the rule, it is a different rule: retention can now delete nothing, and an audit table that can only grow is its own incident. The comment on the block reads 'Faz 3.5 hand-author addition'. WORSE FOR shared.audit_logs: the live set contains no function and no trigger for it at all. The canonical cross-service audit table lost its immutability guarantee outright. WHY THE GUARD DID NOT SAY SO: audit-immutability-triggers.spec.ts asserted the pre-squash SPELLING (ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN for legalHold; specific function names) against a corpus that also included the archived pre-squash files. It was dormant, so its red was unread. FIX. libs/backend-common/src/database/audit-immutability.sql.ts generates the contract from (schema, table) -- four tables across three services, and a migration cannot be shared across services, so the SQL is generated once and each service's migration calls it. Hand-copying is exactly what produced the fifth variant. Three forward-only migrations apply it (admin covers shared + admin; auth; farm, registered in FARM_MIGRATIONS since farm uses an explicit array). Each drops the superseded consolidated trigger by name before creating the pair, and drops the orphaned function only after the trigger using it is gone. down() refuses: dropping these makes audit rows mutable and removes the legal-hold guard. The invariant now asserts the GENERATOR's output (including that DELETE is conditional on legalHold, the half the squash lost) AND that each owning service's effective migration set invokes it for that table -- a correct generator nobody calls being the ORPHAN-HIGH-455 shape. title: ARIA had no tree-level continuity root: per-file hash chains make each ledger tamper-evident but nothing attested that a set of surfaces is one coherent state following a prior one, so losing the whole tree (expired 30-day artifact, runner-local workspace) was indistinguishable from a fresh bootstrap - every surviving file still verified
rule_violated: A control must be able to distinguish the two states it is supposed to act differently on (ORPHAN-CRITICAL-498's class, one level above the files): with only per-file chains, 'fresh bootstrap' and 'total state loss' produce identical verification output, and the closest existing witness (the daily anchor's integrity_index_chain_root) covers only the ~9-name index-group map, not surface presence
notes: Wave 1 PR 2.2 of docs/plans/2026-08-02-aria-full-autonomy-program/PLAN.md. Fixed in the registering commit: state_snapshot.build_snapshot folds every present declared surface (path, sha256, segments, ledger row_count + tail_ledger_hash) into a manifest_root; storage policy is derived from the manifest's own state_class column (ledger/index/runtime_state carried, artifact pinned-only, lock excluded) with an unclassified class raising rather than vanishing; snapshots chain via prev_snapshot_id + prev_manifest_root INSIDE the hashed payload so a continuous history cannot be forged by re-pointing genuine snapshots; snapshot_continuity reports surfaces_lost / chain_broken / genesis; sign_snapshot + verify_snapshot_signature use the existing per-cycle ed25519 identity through ssh-keygen -Y under a dedicated namespace and REFUSE rather than degrade when the binary is absent. Reachable via `aria-kernel state snapshot` / `state verify-snapshot` and consumed by the daily anchor (new state_snapshot_id + state_manifest_root fields), which commits the root outside the store it describes. NOT claimed by this finding and tracked separately: automatic per-cycle snapshot production and publish-time ancestry enforcement land in PR 2.3 (state_store + publish_state FF-only CAS), which is where ORPHAN-CRITICAL-484 and ORPHAN-CRITICAL-513 get the positive-ancestry-proof fix this primitive supplies.

title: Workflow jobs ran aria-kernel code without provisioning aria-kernel: aria-daily-report imported the kernel 27 lines before its pip install, so every scheduled run since 2026-07-17 died on ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'yaml' and the committed daily anchor stopped being produced for 17 days; four more workflows import the kernel with no install step at all
rule_violated: A correctness coupling maintained by hand in eleven places with nothing checking it is not a coupling, it is a coincidence: 'this step runs kernel code' and 'an earlier step installed the kernel' were ordered by hand per job, so a step inserted above the install silently broke a scheduled lane, and four workflows never had an install step at all
notes: Found while checking Wave 0 §0.7's follow-through gate. Watchdog incident issue #1005 (open since 2026-07-17, updated hourly) listed 10 of 14 watched scheduled workflows failing or missing. Fixed in the registering commit: .github/actions/setup-aria-kernel installs the interpreter plus the kernel's declared dependencies from pyproject.toml and verifies importability; all eleven kernel-running jobs use it and their hand-rolled install blocks are deleted; tests/invariants/aria-kernel-workflow-setup.spec.ts fails any job that runs kernel code without an EARLIER uses of that action in the SAME job (positional, per-job, because each job gets a fresh runner) and found 30 violations on first run. Separate cause, NOT fixed by code: aria-auto-cycle and aria-agent-executor declare runs-on [self-hosted, linux, claude] and their runs queue 24h then auto-cancel because that runner is offline - operator action, and it makes Wave 0 §0.7's gate unreachable until the runner returns (PLAN.md corrected in the same commit).

title: The scheduled-workflow watchdog's verdict has no consumer inside ARIA: incident issue #1005 reported ARIA's own nightly loop as not-running every hour for 17 days while the ladder, the merge authority and the program plan all continued as if evidence were accumulating
rule_violated: A signal that no gate consumes is not a control (ORPHAN-CRITICAL-498's family): detection worked perfectly - the watchdog raised and maintained an incident hourly - but nothing in the kernel reads it, so ARIA kept planning, merging and counting readiness while aria-auto-cycle had not run since 2026-07-17
notes: Registered, NOT fixed in the registering commit, and the review file says so explicitly rather than implying otherwise. The consumer belongs with ARIA's own gates (autonomy-ladder progress must not count while a watched ARIA lane is stale; merge authority should refuse autonomous merges under an open ARIA-lane incident), and wiring it wants the durable state store from Wave 1 PR 2.3 so the freeze is recorded durably instead of being recomputed per run. Deadline set two weeks out to land with or immediately after 2.3. Detection itself is sound and must not be duplicated: a second watchdog would be the copy-drift disease, so the fix is a consumer, never another detector.

title: The tree-level continuity root had no consumer: manifest_root was computed, chained and signed, but no gate refused a publish on it, so ARIA gained the evidence for ancestry without gaining the check
rule_violated: A capability with no caller is not a control (ORPHAN-CRITICAL-498's family). PR 2.2 delivered manifest_root plus a signed, chained snapshot; nothing read it. The publish gate went on proving a STEP ('restored=true', the download exited zero) rather than the BYTES, so a tree emptied between restore and publish still satisfied it, and an empty tree passes integrity verify because an empty tree is trivially consistent. build_daily_anchor's state_snapshot_path parameter was likewise unreachable: neither emit_anchor_to_path nor the CLI forwarded to it.
notes: Closed by the registering PR, not deferred: state_store.publish_state refuses unless the snapshot's prev_manifest_root equals the tip's manifest_root, read from the COMMIT (git show HEAD:snapshot.json) rather than the working tree so a caller cannot rewrite what it is checked against; and the daily anchor now receives a derived state_snapshot_path through both levels. Distinct from ORPHAN-CRITICAL-484/488/513, which are about the artifact lane's transport and stay OPEN until the lane cutover (PR 2.4-2.6) — this finding is about the evidence KIND being unused, which is closed the moment one function enforces it and both lanes can only reach the branch through that function.

title: Ledger segment rollover was superseded by measured surface archival, and the consuming trigger does not exist yet: surface sizes are now recorded but nothing reads them, so a surface that does approach an archival threshold will cross it unnoticed
rule_violated: A measurement with no consumer is the same defect class as a capability with no caller: it makes the answer available without making anyone ask the question.
notes: PLAN §2.2b originally specified .seg-NNN rollover at 8 MB with prev_segment_tail_hash continuity rows. A blast-radius map found 42 blocking couplings across roughly 100 readers: path-keyed lock identity, _verify_jsonl_from_text's None chain seed, one-name-one-path index membership, and about 25 workspace readers that resolve a surface to exactly one file. It would also have introduced a fail-OPEN append guard — surface_for_path returns None for a path matching no declared pattern and _assert_raw_jsonl_append_allowed returns on None, which is CORRECT today (an undeclared path is not a governed surface) but becomes a hole the moment segment files hold governed state under undeclared names. Measurement: the largest real ledger on disk is 313 KB against the 8 MB trigger, a factor of 26. The replacement is surface-level archival into an artifact-class file whose sha256 the snapshot already pins, preserving one-live-file-per-surface so no reader changes. PR 2.3 landed the measurement half (size_bytes on every snapshot surface entry, free because the walk already visits each file). This finding tracks the consumer: a threshold check that raises pressure when a surface approaches the archival point. Deliberately NOT urgent — the deadline reflects 26x headroom, not indifference; closing it early with a guessed threshold would be worse than closing it with a series to look at.

title: Two of ARIA's three state roots died with the runner: the workspace surfaces lived under $HOME and aria-findings/ is gitignored and carried nowhere, so every bootstrap restarted finding IDs at F-001 and lost all workspace memory
rule_violated: State that a system reasons about across runs must outlive a run. Ten declared workspace surfaces resolved under the runner's $HOME and six declared repo surfaces under a gitignored directory, so sixteen of ARIA's declared surfaces were structurally incapable of persisting - and nothing said so, because each surviving file still verified.
notes: Named as gap 4 in the program plan but never registered. Closed by binding both roots to the durable store through ONE resolver (workspace.repo_state_root for the repo root; the pre-existing ARIA_WORKSPACE_BASE seam for the workspace root), with state_store.store_environment as the single definition of the binding so a lane cannot get two roots right and the third wrong. gh_token_factory._keys_dir is DELIBERATELY not redirected: per-cycle ed25519 private keys and scoped tokens are credentials, not state, and dying with the runner is their correct lifetime.

title: The state store staged its entire working tree, so redirecting the repo-state root into it would have committed per-cycle ed25519 private keys and scoped installation tokens to a pushed branch
rule_violated: A component that commits and pushes must stage an explicitly enumerated set, never 'everything present'. Enumerating removes the class; an ignore rule only removes the instance, and must be re-added for every future secret.
notes: Found while implementing the root redirection, BEFORE the redirection existed - so it was never exploitable in a shipped state, and this is a near-miss recorded rather than an incident. gh_token_factory writes private keys and tokens to aria-debts/keys/, immediately beside the declared aria-debts/ ledgers. The main checkout's .gitignore covers that path but does NOT reach inside a worktree whose top level is store_dir (git reads no .gitignore above a worktree root), and publish_state used `git add --all --force`, which overrides ignore rules anyway. Closed by staging exactly the snapshot's own surface paths plus the two markers: an undeclared file cannot be committed because nothing names it. Two further properties fall out - the commit is bound to the attestation by construction rather than merely consistent with it, and the previous snapshot's paths are included so a surface that VANISHED can still stage as a deletion.

title: Re-observing unchanged evidence re-raised belief confidence, so ARIA read its own repetition as corroboration: one unchanged file carried a belief from 0.605 to 0.925 in eleven cycles
rule_violated: Confidence must track evidence, not observation count. A system that re-reads the same file every cycle and treats each read as new support is measuring its own schedule, not the world.
notes: Named as gap 6 in the program plan. TWO mechanisms, and fixing either alone leaves a ratchet: support_count incremented unconditionally, AND the support term is added to previous_confidence rather than to the original, so it compounds on the already-raised value. Both are now gated on evidence_hashes differing from the stored row's; both halves are mutation-checked separately (restoring the unconditional increment fails 2 tests, restoring the unconditional term fails 1). Learning is not frozen - changed evidence still increments support and still raises confidence, with a test for that. Occurrence is retained as observation_count, in a field nothing reads into confidence. Three existing tests in test_enterprise_cycle.py asserted the old behaviour and were rewritten to their real intent rather than deleted: each gained a sharper assertion (equality instead of 'confidence rose'), because the property they actually protect holds MORE strongly once the ratchet is gone.

title: A CONVERGED plan was recorded as a 0.9-confidence convention before any outcome existed, and MIN_PATTERN_CONFIDENCE is 0.7 — so ARIA served its own untested predictions to the next planner as established knowledge
rule_violated: A prediction is not a fact. Knowledge recorded before an outcome exists must not be served at the same confidence as knowledge an outcome confirmed, or the system compounds its own guesses into its own priors.
notes: Named as gap 7 in the program plan. The convention row is written when the convergent gate resolves - before merge, before CI has run against the change, before any outcome exists - and 0.9 sits above lookup_pattern's 0.7 serving floor, so it was immediately handed to later planners as established knowledge. Convergence IS evidence (planner, challenger and cross-review agreed) but evidence about AGREEMENT, not about outcome. Closed by recording the row at CONVENTION_HYPOTHESIS_CONFIDENCE=0.5 with outcome_status='hypothesis': stored, because the observation is worth keeping, and below the floor, so it is not served. Pattern.outcome_status defaults to 'unknown' rather than 'verified' - every convention written before this field existed was also pre-outcome, and defaulting them to verified would assert something the ledger never observed. Promotion to 'verified' on a VERIFIED mission and demotion on a rolled-back one is Wave 10's half; this is the half that stops the false claim. Both halves mutation-checked.

title: A required merge gate depended on a live third-party chart registry being reachable at that instant, in two hand-copied callsites: one TCP reset from charts.bitnami.com failed pre-flight and took build-status with it on a PR that touched no infrastructure, and the workflow token cannot re-run a failed job so recovery required pushing an unrelated commit
rule_violated: A single-shot network fetch inside a merge gate is a coin flip the gate has to win every time. `charts/` is build output rather than source, so every renderer must resolve subchart archives from upstream at CI time; spelled as two hand-written `run:` lines with no retry, that put an external CDN's momentary availability on the critical path of a branch-protection-required check, and the same defect had to be fixed twice or not at all.
notes: Observed, not theorised: run 30798949933 on PR #1056. Fixed in the registering commit by one composite action used by both callsites, with bounded retry (3 attempts, 5s then 10s) and a ::warning:: per retry so flakiness stays countable rather than silent. The retry lives in resolve.sh rather than inline in the action's run: block for a testability reason that is the point of the design — inline, the only available assertion is that the words 'attempt' and 'sleep' appear in the YAML, which a loop that never increments its counter also satisfies; as a script it is run against a stub helm and the tests count invocations (1 call on first success, 2 on one transient, exactly 3 when the registry is down, exactly 5 under ATTEMPTS=5, 0 under ATTEMPTS=0 and 0 on a missing Chart.yaml). Six mutations each fail at least one test. NOT taken and named rather than left implied: vendoring the resolved .tgz archives would remove the network entirely and is structurally stronger, but it inverts the convention this chart states explicitly (Chart.yaml is the SSoT, charts/ is build output) and committed archives that drift from their pinned versions have no detector except fetching from the network - that trade is an infrastructure-ownership decision with an ADR's weight, not a side effect of unblocking a merge queue. The invariant tripped over its own documentation twice on first run (comments, then the step's name: label) and one mutation initially SURVIVED because the assertion checked for any ::warning:: while the retry notice satisfied it; both messages are now pinned by content.

title: Nothing consumed tree-level continuity before a cycle acted: a bootstrap-empty aria-tools/ and a restored one were the same observation to everything downstream, and an empty tree passes integrity verify because an empty tree is trivially consistent
rule_violated: A control must be able to distinguish the two states it is supposed to act differently on, and the evidence for that distinction cannot live inside the thing being judged: a tree that lost its history also lost any record that it had one, so no file under aria-tools/ can answer whether aria-tools/ is complete. PR 2.1 gave the tree a manifest, 2.2 a chained manifest_root, 2.3 a publish-time refusal - and none of them was read before a cycle planned, learned or counted acceptance evidence on the tree.

Closed in the registering commit: memory_gap.assess_memory_continuity compares a snapshot of the tree the cycle opened on against a reference resolved OUTSIDE it (the aria/state branch tip first, then the daily anchors committed under aria-tools/reports/daily/), and a new preflight stage runs it before discovery. THREE verdicts, and the third is load-bearing: unknown is neither ok nor critical, returned whenever no reference exists, because guessing continuous re-opens the hole and guessing amnesiac would refuse every cycle on this repository today - every committed anchor predates state_manifest_root and the newest two are hand-written markdown with no frontmatter. Stated plainly rather than buried: on main today this gate reports unknown every night and blocks nothing; it starts refusing when either reference becomes real (the daily anchor lane resuming, or the state-store lane cutover in PR 2.6). ONE freeze mechanism: record_failure(kind='state_integrity_gap'), a new closed-taxonomy FAILURE_KINDS member, because _cycle_preflight already consults the breaker for every profile in PROFILES_WITH_ACTION_AUTHORITY - a separate frozen flag would be a second answer to how ARIA stops, which is what ORPHAN-CRITICAL-513 cost. freeze_autonomous_writes RAISES on any status but critical, so an unproven gap structurally cannot trip a breaker. No workflow edit ships: a second early check duplicating what the action enforces is the copy-drift this wave keeps treating. restore_and_replay moves to PR 2.6 with the lane that gives it a transport; equivalence_check ships here because 2.6 needs it and it is testable standalone. Two existing gates failed on first run by design and were edited as the reviewed decisions they demand: the breaker-producer allowlist gained memory_gap.py, and the pinned burn-in phase set gained state_continuity (burn-in's output IS the acceptance evidence the ladder counts, so evidence gathered on a tree that forgot its history is exactly what must not count).

title: A lost publish race left the losing lane's rows stranded: publish_state correctly refused and rolled back, but the caller was told to fetch and rebuild by hand and on the scheduled lanes there is no such caller, so the rows sat in a worktree nothing revisits
rule_violated: A correct refusal that leaves work stranded is still work stranded. publish_state is a compare-and-swap against a fast-forward-only branch, so the second of two lanes publishing from one tip is rejected by the server; PR 2.3 made that refusal safe (rollback, rows staged, nothing overwritten) but left the recovery as a manual instruction in an error message, on lanes that run unattended.
notes: Wave 1 PR 2.6 of docs/plans/2026-08-02-aria-full-autonomy-program/PLAN.md. Closed in the registering commit. The common prefix is PROVEN, not assumed: every ledger row carries a ledger_hash over the whole chain behind it and the base snapshot records each surface's row_count + tail_ledger_hash, so 'do these two files share their first N rows' is answered by requiring the row at index N-1 to carry the base tail hash in BOTH files - a match there implies the whole prefix matches. Anything else is a rewrite wearing an append's clothes and is refused; the resolution is deliberately not a git merge, because -X ours/-X theirs would silently drop one lane's rows, which is ORPHAN-CRITICAL-484's outcome by another road. The winner is checked against the base too, and that check initially had no real test: a refusal asserted with a base hash matching NEITHER tree came from the loser's check, and mutating the winner's check away left all twelve tests green - the isolating test now has the loser descending cleanly and only the winner diverging. Order is the safety property: the loser's ledgers are copied out BEFORE the worktree is reset, so rows are never only in memory across a destructive git operation. Replayed rows are re-chained rather than copied. Replay is NOT idempotent by construction and a failing test found that (a retry against a stale base duplicated every row); the guard is a tail match on logical content rather than set membership, because two lanes can legitimately emit similar rows. TWO PLAN CORRECTIONS: the advisory publish lease from PLAN 2.6 is deliberately NOT built - with replay the race is correct and cheap, and an advisory lease adds a second coordination mechanism whose stale-lease failure mode is worse than the problem, a second answer to 'who may publish' being the pattern this wave spent five PRs removing; and a store-checked-out tools root cannot be used until bound, because repo_identity.json is machine-local binding state (absolute bound_repo_root) and so is not a declared surface, leaving a fresh checkout in exactly the ambiguous_tools_root shape - the governed binding step is integrity migrate-tools-bootstrap, the same step PLAN 2.5 wanted deleted, which is the second and stronger reason it stays.

title: Adapter candidate confidence fails open to maximum certainty: tool_runner._valid_memory_candidates accepts any non-negative number and clamps it with min(float(confidence), 1.0), so an adapter emitting a count, severity grade, or milliseconds reading as confidence is silently promoted to 1.0 and flows into memory._record_belief as the belief's starting weight
rule_violated: Out-of-range input on a trust surface must be refused, not coerced toward maximum trust. instinct_candidate.py already draws the line correctly (raise GovernanceError outside [0,1]); tool_runner disagrees in the opposite direction, and the disagreement fails open: min(float(confidence), 1.0) turns a unit error into certainty. The two modules answer 'what does an out-of-range confidence mean' differently, which is the two-answers defect this program keeps removing.
notes: Found while grounding the mathematical-kernel proposal review (PLAN 4d.1) against the tree. Fix shape is tier 1 (make it impossible): a validating Confidence construction path per kind - pattern score, belief weight, judge probability, adapter score, instinct score - that refuses out-of-range input the way instinct_candidate already does. The clamp is deleted, not widened. Scheduled into Wave 2's first schema PR (mission.py PR 1.1) because the fix touches the adapter candidate contract, not one callsite; the closing commit carries Closes against this row. Related but distinct: judge_calibration's else-branch assumes the FEEDBACK_VERDICTS pair is complementary, so a third verdict added later would silently count as false_positive - scheduled as PLAN 4d.3 (Wave 4) and noted here so the two do not merge into one fix.
